input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-352: Operating Systems. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: An in-depth study of operating system concepts. Topics include process synchronization, interprocess communication, deadlock, multiprogramming and multiprocessing, processor scheduling and resource management, memory management, static and dynamic relocation, virtual memory, file systems, logical and physical I/O, device allocation, I/O processor scheduling, process and resource protection. Programming projects involving the development of or modification to operating system kernel features will be required. Prerequisites: CSCI-250 or CMPE-350 or SWEN-340 or equivalent course. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall

Source excerpts:

[mit-xv6-book]
The xv6 book explains processes, system calls, traps, page tables, scheduling, locking, file systems, devices, concurrency, and isolation in a small Unix-like kernel. A process combines an address space with execution state and operating-system resources. A system call transfers control from user code to a privileged kernel service. A trap records processor state so the kernel can handle a system call, exception, or interrupt. Page tables map virtual addresses to physical memory with permission bits. The scheduler selects runnable processes and switches processor context. Locks protect invariants when concurrent execution can access shared state. The file system organizes persistent data through inodes, directories, and logged updates. Analysis distinguishes user mode, privileged kernel code, hardware translation, interrupt state, resource ownership, and synchronization invariants.

[riscv-unprivileged]
The RISC-V ISA defines programmer-visible instructions, registers, memory operations, control transfer, exceptions, and ordering behavior. Integer register x0 always reads as zero, while the remaining integer registers hold software-visible values. Load instructions transfer data from memory into registers. Store instructions transfer register data to memory. Branch and jump instructions change control flow. Exceptions report conditions that require a defined transfer of control. Memory-ordering rules constrain how memory operations may be observed. Architecture analysis preserves data dependencies, control dependencies, and architectural state.

[rit-csci-352]
An in-depth study of operating system concepts. Topics include process synchronization, interprocess communication, deadlock, multiprogramming and multiprocessing, processor scheduling and resource management, memory management, static and dynamic relocation, virtual memory, file systems, logical and physical I/O, device allocation, I/O processor scheduling, process and resource protection. Programming projects involving the development of or modification to operating system kernel features will be required. Prerequisites: CSCI-250 or CMPE-350 or SWEN-340 or equivalent course. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall

beats.claim: A process combines an address space with execution state and operating-system resources.
beats.example: A running web server process maintains its own stack, heap, and open file descriptors while executing user-level code.
beats.title: Process Model & State
beats.visualDirection: Show a diagram of a process with labeled components: address space, execution state, and resource ownership. Annotate each component with its function in the OS model.

beats.claim: A system call transfers control from user code to a privileged kernel service.
beats.example: When a program requests disk I/O, it executes a system call instruction that switches execution to the kernel to handle the request.
beats.title: System Calls & Privilege Levels
beats.visualDirection: Display a flowchart showing user mode code calling a system call, transitioning to kernel mode, and returning to user mode with a result.

beats.claim: A trap records processor state so the kernel can handle a system call, exception, or interrupt.
beats.example: When a page fault occurs, the CPU traps the faulting instruction, saves the instruction pointer and registers, and transfers control to the kernel handler.
beats.title: Traps & Processor State
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a trap sequence with arrows showing state capture, kernel entry, exception handling, and state restoration.

beats.claim: Page tables map virtual addresses to physical memory with permission bits.
beats.example: A page table entry for a read-only code segment contains a valid bit, a present bit, and a read-only permission flag.
beats.title: Page Tables & Virtual Memory
beats.visualDirection: Show a page table structure with columns for virtual address, physical address, and permission bits, highlighting how mappings are resolved.

beats.claim: The scheduler selects runnable processes and switches processor context.
beats.example: The OS scheduler picks a ready process from the run queue, saves the current process's registers, and loads the new process's context.
beats.title: Processor Scheduling
beats.visualDirection: Draw a scheduler loop with states: ready queue, running, blocked, and context switch arrows between processes.

beats.claim: Locks protect invariants when concurrent execution can access shared state.
beats.example: A mutex lock ensures that only one thread can modify a shared counter at a time, preventing race conditions.
beats.title: Locks & Synchronization
beats.visualDirection: Show a lock acquisition/release sequence with two concurrent threads, highlighting mutual exclusion and invariant protection.

beats.claim: Deadlock occurs when concurrent processes wait for each other's resources, violating resource ownership invariants.
beats.example: Two processes each hold one file descriptor and wait for the other's, creating a circular dependency that halts progress.
beats.title: Deadlock & Resource Management
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a deadlock scenario with two processes and two resources, showing circular wait arrows and resource ownership.

beats.claim: Multiprogramming and multiprocessing allow multiple processes to execute concurrently by sharing processor resources.
beats.example: A server handles multiple client requests simultaneously by switching between processes on a single CPU core.
beats.title: Multiprogramming & Multiprocessing
beats.visualDirection: Show a CPU core with multiple process contexts interleaved, emphasizing time-sharing and resource allocation.

beats.claim: The file system organizes persistent data through inodes, directories, and logged updates.
beats.example: A directory entry points to an inode that stores file metadata, permissions, and block addresses for data storage.
beats.title: File Systems & I/O
beats.visualDirection: Display a file system tree with directories, inodes, and block clusters, showing how data is organized and updated.

beats.claim: Students must verify that user mode, privileged kernel code, hardware translation, interrupt state, resource ownership, and synchronization invariants are correctly implemented.
beats.example: Audit a kernel module to ensure all shared variables are protected by locks and that page table permissions match access rights.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Provide a checklist graphic with checkboxes for each invariant: user/kernel mode, hardware translation, interrupt handling, resource ownership, and synchronization.

learningObjectives: Define and explain the operational model of a process, including its address space, execution state, and resource ownership.

Explain how locks and synchronization mechanisms protect shared state invariants during concurrent execution, and identify common deadlock conditions.
